content: Ready-to-use lipid-based nutrient supplements (LNS) are highly nutrient-dense formulations designed to provide both macronutrients and micronutrients. These supplements are particularly beneficial for pregnant women who require additional nutritional support to meet their dietary needs. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of LNS on maternal health, birth outcomes, and infant development. Secondary objectives included determining the optimal composition, frequency, and duration of LNS administration. A comprehensive search was conducted in May 2018 across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and 22 others, as well as two trial registries. Reference lists of included studies and relevant reviews were also examined, and authors of included studies and field experts were contacted to identify any additional or unpublished studies. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that compared LNS supplementation during pregnancy to no intervention, placebo, iron-folic acid (IFA), multiple micronutrients (MMN), or nutritional counseling. Standard Cochrane methodologies were employed for data collection and analysis. Four studies involving a total of 8,018 pregnant women were included. These studies were conducted in stable community settings in lowand middle-income countries, specifically Bangladesh, Burkina Faso, Ghana, and Malawi. None of the studies were conducted in emergency settings. The earliest study was published in 2009. Among the four studies, one compared LNS to IFA, one compared LNS to MMN, and two compared LNS to both IFA and MMN. The studies were assessed to be of medium to high quality, and the evidence was rated as moderate using the GRADE approach. LNS versus IFA: Maternal Outcomes: There was no significant difference between the LNS and IFA groups in terms of maternal gestational weight gain per week (SMD 0.46, 95% CI −0.44 to 1.36; 2 studies, 3,539 participants). However, one study (536 participants) reported a two-fold increase in the prevalence of maternal anemia in the LNS group compared to the IFA group. No differences were observed between the groups regarding adverse effects or maternal mortality (RR 0.53, 95% CI 0.12 to 2.41; 3 studies, 5,628 participants). Birth and Infant Outcomes: There was no significant difference between the LNS and IFA groups for low birth weight (LBW) (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.05; 3 studies, 4,826 participants). However, newborns in the LNS group had a slightly higher mean birth weight (MD 53.28 g, 95% CI 28.22 to 78.33; 3 studies, 5,077 participants) and birth length (MD 0.24 cm, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.36; 3 studies, 4,986 participants). The LNS group also showed a reduction in the proportion of infants who were small for gestational age (SGA) (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.89 to 0.99; 3 studies, 4,823 participants) and those with newborn stunting (RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.71 to 0.94; 2 studies, 4,166 participants). No differences were observed between the groups for preterm delivery (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.11; 4 studies, 4,924 participants), stillbirth (RR 1.14, 95% CI 0.52 to 2.48; 3 studies, 5,575 participants), or neonatal death (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.14 to 6.51). Evidence regarding child developmental outcomes was insufficient to draw firm conclusions. LNS versus MMN: Maternal Outcomes: One study (662 participants) found no significant difference between the LNS and MMN groups in terms of gestational weight gain per week or adverse effects. Another study (557 participants) reported an increased risk of maternal anemia in the LNS group compared to the MMN group. Birth and Infant Outcomes: There were no significant differences between the LNS and MMN groups for LBW (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.14; 3 studies, 2,404 participants), birth weight (MD 23.67 g, 95% CI −10.53 to 57.86; 3 studies, 2,573 participants), birth length (MD 0.20 cm, 95% CI −0.02 to 0.42; 3 studies, 2,567 participants), SGA (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.07; 3 studies, 2,393 participants), preterm delivery (RR 1.15, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.42; 3 studies, 2,630 participants), head circumference z-score (MD 0.10, 95% CI −0.01 to 0.21; 2 studies, 1,549 participants), or neonatal death (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.36 to 2.15; 1 study, 1,175 participants). Conclusions: The findings suggest that LNS supplementation has a modest positive effect on birth weight, birth length, SGA, and newborn stunting compared to IFA. However, LNS and MMN were comparable for all maternal, birth, and infant outcomes. Both IFA and MMN were more effective than LNS in reducing maternal anemia. No studies were identified that evaluated the use of LNS in emergency settings. The beneficial findings should be interpreted with caution due to the limited number of trials, with one large-scale study conducted in Bangladesh driving most of the observed effects. Additionally, the effect sizes were small, making it difficult to propose concrete recommendations for clinical practice.
